newsitem.title: THAILAND: Amnesty urges Thailand not to push back Karen.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty urges Thailand not to push back Karen.

text.p: Amnesty International on Thursday urged Thailand to halt any forcible return of Karen refugees who had fled to the Thai side after recent fighting between Burmese troops and rebel Karen National Union (KNU) guerrillas.

"Ethnic Karens...who may not be allowed to seek refuge in neighbouring Thailand or are returned to Burma are at risk of ill-treatment, being taken as porters or possible unlawful killing by the Burmese army," the London-based human rights organisation said in a statement.
But Thai military sources said the refugees merely were moved to safer places in Thailand away from fighting.
The KNU has been fighting the Burmese government since 1948 for greater autonomy for the Karen state.

Burmese troops overran KNU bases in eastern Karen state earlier this month, forcing civilians to flee. The Burmese military said this week it was prepared to take back those Karen refugees willing to return to the country.
Thailand has housed more than 70,000 Karen refugees in camps along the border with Burma since the early 1980's.

Amnesty said several thousand Karen refugees had fled into Thailand's Kanchanaburi province. But the Thai military told the refugees they could stay only three days, after which the men would be sent back to the conflict area and the women and children to a "safe corridor" further south along the border.
"Unofficial sources dispute that the safe corridor is secure given movements of the Burmese army," Amnesty said.
Thai authorities had on February 24 and 25 refused entry to 730 Karen men, but allowed in women, children and the disabled.

"The remaining 600 women and children were put on trucks and taken to Amphur Suan Pung located further south in Ratchaburi province, opposite the safe corridor area, from where it is believed they may be forcibly repatriated...," Amnesty said.
Thailand had also told hundreds of other Karen refugees in camps in Sangklaburi province, north of Kanchanaburi, to return to Burma or agree to be taken to the safe corridor, it said.

The group called on Thailand to adhere to the international principle of "non-refoulement", which prohibits states from returning refugees against their will to countries where they risk serious human rights violations.
Amnesty also urged Thailand to halt any forcible return of Karen refugees and grant them protection instead.
A Thai military source told Reuters they had not forcibly returned any Karen refugee, but were preventing men suspected of being KNU guerrillas from entering the country.

"When the refugees are being put on to trucks, it is not to send them back but to move them to a safer location inside Thailand's Pangwau village near the border," the source said by telephone from the border area.

Said KNU Captain Marshalle, who is based at the border near Kanchanaburi: "They (the Thai military) "merely relocated about 1,500 refugees who have been living in the border to other locations deeper inside Thailand, not pushed back."
